claim: An eight-item classifier trained on ADOS Module 1 scores from the Autism Genetic Resource Exchange diagnoses autism as accurately as the full 29-item Module 1, so the same shortened instrument can screen children for autism outside the clinic.
primary_study: Wall, Kosmicki, DeLuca, Harstad & Fusaro, 2012, Translational Psychiatry
provenance: Kapoor §2.4 names Bone's case. Primary is Wall et al. 2012 (ADOS Module 1; PMC3337074). Claim written from Wall's abstract and stated aim. The review row also carries L1.4; this entry stands for L3.3, the named case.

claim: A model trained on clinical records of obstetric admissions can identify adverse drug events during labor and delivery, so the same model can flag at-risk deliveries at other hospitals.
primary_study: Taft, Evans, Shyu, Egger, Chawla & Mitchell, 2009, J Biomed Inform
provenance: Named by Blagus & Lusa (PMC4634915) as a biomedical prediction task. Claim written from the study's title and topic (ADE prediction in labor and delivery), not from Blagus's account of how sampling was applied.

claim: Read-across models trained on a database of chemical properties and hazards assembled from ECHA REACH dossiers can predict nine UN GHS health hazards for a compound at accuracy matching or exceeding the reproducibility of repeat OECD guideline animal tests, so the same models can classify untested commercial chemicals without new animal studies.
primary_study: Luechtefeld, Marsh, Rowlands & Hartung, 2018, Toxicol Sci (RASAR)
provenance: Alves is a comment on Luechtefeld et al. Claim written from Luechtefeld's abstract (PMC6135638), not from the comment.

claim: A sum-of-squared-correlations spatial filter, fit to a subject's SSVEP templates, detects which of 40 flickering visual targets the subject is attending to from EEG, outperforming task-related component analysis on a 35-person benchmark, so the same decoder can drive an SSVEP-based BCI speller.
primary_study: Kiran Kumar & Ramasubba Reddy, 2019, IEEE TNSRE (SSCOR)
provenance: Nakanishi's comment title names the primary. Claim written from the SSCOR paper's abstract (doi:10.1109/tnsre.2019.2941349), not from Nakanishi's criticism.

claim: An Inception-v3 network trained on TCGA whole-slide images of non-small cell lung cancer classifies adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma and predicts commonly mutated genes (STK11, EGFR, FAT1, SETBP1, KRAS, TP53) from the histopathology image, so the same network can infer mutation status from a diagnostic slide without sequencing.
provenance: Oner (doi:10.1101/2020.04.23.20076406) names Coudray et al. as the study re-analysed. Claim written from Coudray's published abstract, not from Oner's account of how slides were split.

claim: An XGBoost model trained on the previous year's records from the Maine Health Information Exchange can predict which patients will receive a new diagnosis of essential hypertension within one year, so the same model can stratify patients in that statewide network for early intervention.
provenance: Kapoor §2.4 names Filho's case. Primary is Ye et al. (PMC5811646). Claim written from Ye's stated aim (incident essential hypertension from prior-year statewide EHR), not from Filho's feature-level criticism.

claim: A support-vector model trained on resting-state EEG recorded at baseline and two weeks after starting escitalopram can predict whether an adult with major depressive disorder will respond by week 8 (a 50% drop in MADRS), using data from the CAN-BIND-1 multicenter study, so the same model can be used to choose an antidepressant at a new clinic.
primary_study: Zhdanov et al., 2020, JAMA Network Open
provenance: Shim (PMC8042090) names Zhdanov et al. as the recent study. Claim written from Zhdanov's abstract and methods (PMC6991244), not from Shim's account of how features were selected.

claim: VulDeePecker, a deep network that represents C/C++ programs as code gadgets — semantically related lines of code transformed into vectors — detects software vulnerabilities without hand-crafted features, and when applied to Xen, Seamonkey, and Libav it finds vulnerabilities that were later silently patched, so the same detector can scan other C/C++ codebases.
provenance: Arp §4.2 reproduces VulDeePecker. The Kapoor table row carries six types; this entry is a single-type conversion standing for L2 only. L2 was chosen because Arp's finding on this system is classification on tokens that are not a vulnerability signal (illegitimate features), a different L2 instantiation from Filho/Ye. Scoring the row as a hit on any of six would not test whether the tool surfaces the question this case poses. Claim written from Li et al.'s abstract (arx_1801.01681), not from Arp's pitfall analysis.

source_review: Tu et al., 2018; Lyu et al., 2021
provenance: L3.1 (temporal leakage) appears only on Tu 2018 and Lyu 2021, both unread IEEE. Not convertible. Documented gap in the suite, not a missing score.
